description: ClimateX is a team passionate about Artificial Intelligence, Data Science, and innovation. We transform environmental data into meaningful insights to better understand climate change and its impact on our planet. Through data analysis, statistical methods, and AI technologies, our goal is to develop innovative, data-driven solutions that contribute to a more sustainable future.
summary: I built an interactive web dashboard that turns NASA POWER daily data into clear evidence of climate change in Moroccan cities (Casablanca, Fez, Marrakech, Tetouan, Essaouira and Berkane). A Python FastAPI backend collects and cleans the data, then applies the seasonal Mann-Kendall test and Sen’s slope to detect trends in maximum temperature, humidity and precipitation, and checks whether each trend is statistically significant. A React frontend lets users explore the results through an interactive map, charts, filters (variable, period, season, significance level) and city-to-city comparisons. Users can even add a new location with one click on the map.
details:
What it does and how it works
Climate Trends is a full-stack web application that detects and compares long-term climate trends in several Moroccan cities using daily NASA POWER data (maximum temperature, relative humidity and precipitation). The backend downloads the data through the NASA POWER API, cleans it (missing-value codes, rebuilt dates, duplicates, incomplete months) and aggregates it monthly. It then applies the seasonal Mann-Kendall test to detect a trend and Sen’s slope to measure how fast the variable changes (per year and per decade), with a p-value to check statistical significance. The React interface displays the results on an interactive map (red = significant increase, blue = significant decrease, grey = no significant trend), in sortable tables, and in charts for each city and for city-to-city comparison.

Benefits
Instead of reading raw data files, users see within seconds where the climate is changing, how fast, and whether the change is statistically reliable. Filters for variable, period, season or month, and significance level let anyone explore the data without coding. Results can be exported as CSV.

Intended impact
The goal is to make local climate evidence accessible to students, researchers and decision-makers, supporting water management, agriculture and climate-adaptation planning in a region highly exposed to heat and drought.

Tools and technologies
Backend: Python, FastAPI, pandas, NumPy, pymannkendall, httpx. Frontend: React, Vite, Leaflet (maps), Recharts (charts). Data source: NASA POWER API. Version control: Git and GitHub. No special hardware is required.

Creativity
The map is not only a display: users click anywhere on it to add a new location, and the app downloads and analyses its data automatically. An anomaly view makes cities with very different climates comparable, and users can test trends by season or by single month to see, for example, whether summers warm faster than winters.

Factors considered
We focused on statistical rigour (seasonality, significance threshold chosen by the user, a warning when a series is shorter than 10 years), data quality, and clarity for non-experts. We also considered limits: NASA POWER combines satellite and model data rather than ground-station measurements, and a statistical trend alone does not prove its cause.
